doc.title: Michael Moore interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

title: From avant-garde experiments to songs with Braff and Barnes
summary: Moore recalls The Space loft scene and free music, then says the Braff-Barnes quartet returned him to songs and tighter forms.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: Yeah well Marian and I talked about that recently, and three or four of my tunes were on there, and they were pretty avante garde. I was kind of in that era of player at the time, and Marian, always wanting to be young musically and keep up with what’s going on, surrounded herself with young players and wanted to get into what they were into. But it’s funny, after that, with me I kind of spent my time in that group of people, like we had a space, it was called The Space, and it was a bunch of musicians and we all shared it and we put on our own concerts in a loft and things like that. And there was a lot of experimental music. Dave Liebman came out of that and Richie Bierach, and a very lot of avante garde things. Right at that time I started playing with Ruby Braff and George Barnes. And I’d grown up playing a lot of traditional music with my father. But you know you’re wrapped up with what your peers are doing, and we played a lot of free music and so forth. And I think when I got with Ruby and George and played in that quartet and everything, it kind of re-set me in a way, in a more — not that I stopped playing the other kind of music — but I think in a way it set me, and made me realize how important songs were to me. Songs from the 30s and 40s in particular, with the great songwriters, because that’s what they were interested in, was the love of it, the American popular songs. And I think that that really, in a way, brought me back inside more. And I haven’t really left that since then. I still really feel that I did my experimentation and I feel now that, as far as like trying that, I feel it was done about as well as it can be done by a lot of players that I loved at that time, in the 60s and around then, and some of the guys are still around, and some of the wonderful Paul Bley, Gary Peacock, and that kind of music.
It’s always been a struggle with that kind of music, as far as your audience reception to it I think. I don’t know if after a while you say maybe this isn’t valid for anyone except myself perhaps.

Well I think it’s a lot more fun to do than it is to listen to. I think that’s one of the problems with the music, with a lot of that. It can become very self-indulgent. And when I started playing with Ruby and George, everything was thought of as — solos weren’t too long — they used Benny’s trios and quartets as a good example of where nobody played too long, there were no 40 chorus solos, and musicians were standing around talking to one another. It was thought out with the audience in mind, but also from, I don’t think as much with the audience in mind, just a real definite feeling about form and

melody and shape — as much as whether the audience is going to like it or not. And I got wrapped up in that too, and it’s to the point now where I can’t stand — as a bass player sometimes I find myself in those situations where the horn players are playing chorus after chorus after chorus, and I’m getting bored, so I can imagine how the audience is feeling. Because I’ve got something to do. And I really think the discipline of that kind of thing is really important in a player, is to — Lester Young could compose in eight bars, something that you can study the rest of your life. He didn’t need 30 or 40 choruses to say something. And I think a lot of that got lost in certain periods of exploration. So I don’t see that I actually regressed, I see it that I progressed out of that kind of experimentation, and went back to thinking about tighter forms and things.
